title: Leadership Handbook: Team Meetings
author: Nick Hart
summary: This piece reframes team meetings not as logistical necessities but as primary mechanisms through which leadership actually happens in schools. Rather than viewing meetings as forums for sharing information and moving through agendas, the author argues they simultaneously accomplish six overlapping forms of work: establishing direction, achieving alignment across roles and timescales, constructing shared understanding of problems, enabling commitment to action, making decisions with clear accountability, and building psychological safety. Ineffective meetings actively undermine school culture by narrowing attention and fragmenting understanding; productive meetings increase the quality of attention across the organization. The framework shifts the leader's role toward shaping interactions that enable better conversations and decisions to emerge.
points: Team meetings are primary mechanisms for leadership, not logistical necessities; they accomplish six simultaneous forms of work including direction, alignment, sense-making, commitment, decision-making, and psychological safety.
Leadership is a feature of the collective, not the individual, making the design of meeting interactions a core leadership responsibility.
Ineffective meetings actively undermine organizational culture by narrowing what is noticed, fragmenting understanding, and weakening follow-through.
The task of the leader shifts from having answers to shaping conditions where better conversations and collective decisions can emerge.
Overlapping conditions in meetings either strengthen or weaken the organization's culture over time, making meeting design strategically important to school improvement.
quotes: Team meetings are often treated as a logistical necessity: a place to share information, review actions or move through an agenda. In practice, this underestimates their role.
In complex organisations like schools, team meetings are one of the primary mechanisms through which leadership actually happens.
Leadership, understood as the social processes from which direction, alignment and commitment emerge, is a feature of the collective, not the individual.
This model reframes team meetings as doing six kinds of work simultaneously: Direction, Alignment, Sense making, Commitment, Decision making, Psychological safety.

Productive meetings increase the quality of attention across the organisation. They help people see patterns more clearly, understand interdependence and act with greater coherence.” Archived from Nick Hart on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
